## The 64th square {#ss6-square-64 .gs-lesson .gs-rice-scale}

How many grains would be on the final square?

::: {.fragment .gs-last-square data-fragment-index="0"}

$$a_{64}=2^{63}=9\,223\,372\,036\,854\,775\,808$$

About **9.22 quintillion grains** on that square alone.

:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway .gs-counting-time data-fragment-index="1"}

Count **one grain per second**, without stopping.

It would take about **292 billion years** — roughly **21 times the age of the universe**.

:::

::: {.fragment .gs-whole-board data-fragment-index="2"}

Across the whole board:

$$S_{64}=2^{64}-1\approx1.84\times10^{19}\text{ grains}$$

:::

::: notes

Allow about 1 minute. Ask students why the exponent for square 64 is 63 before the first click reveals the count. Second click gives a comparison for that single square, not the whole board. At one grain per second, 2^63/(60×60×24×365.25) ≈ 292,271,023,045 years. Compared with the universe's approximate age of 13.8 billion years, this is about 21.2 times as long. These are calculated comparisons using a 365.25-day year; the age is from NASA's Universe Overview. Do not claim that the number of grains exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe.

Third click returns to the lesson's distinction between a term and a sum. The exact total is 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 grains. Ask why the whole-board formula has exponent 64. The preceding activity conjectured this sum rule; the next examples justify the geometric-sum formula.

Sources: https://www.physics.umd.edu/perg/abp/TPProbs/Problems/G/G30.htm (2^63 on the last square and 2^64−1 altogether); https://science.nasa.gov/universe/overview/ (approximate age 13.8 billion years).

:::
